title: Three‑Point Engineer‑Seller Cheat Briefing (draft)
content:
Objective: one-sheet, engineer-facing briefing for SEs running ~15–25 minute pilot conversations. Keep it scannable, confident, and repeatable. This is a working draft — two-sided: conversation script + mini battlecard for quick objections and canary checks.

Topline framing (what to say in 20s):
- "We help engineering teams run LLM inference with predictable latency and unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. In pilots we focus on a single measurable win: lower 95th percentile latency or lower per-token cost by X% while keeping output quality within an agreed tolerance."

Three‑point playbook (core hooks for engineers)
1) Predictable Performance (squeezed into a single sentence)
   - Why it matters: product features die when tail latency spikes or KV-cache misses degrade UX.
   - SE script: "We run a runtime that optimizes kernels, KV cache and continuous batching so your 95th latency stays within target even during bursts. We map your sequence-length distribution, then suggest a compact execution plan you can test in 48h."
   - Evidence to cite (quick lines): preflight profiling, sample latency profile, 1–2 customer anonymized numbers. Keep specifics ready to paste.

2) Operational Control (dev-friendly guardrails)
   - Why it matters: teams want control over degradation, fallbacks, and cost.
   - SE script: "You get routing policies, version pinning, and automated fallbacks — same API across hosted, dedicated and VPC private. So you can canary model changes and have automatic fallback to a cheaper or lower-latency variant if the new model regresses."
   - Demo hook: show the Console route selector and a canary rollout with automatic percentage shift.

3) Cost‑first Fallbacks (sensible defaults that avoid surprise bills)
   - Why it matters: CFOs and infra teams panic at token spikes.
   - SE script: "We propose a fallback ladder: smaller quantized variant, lower temperature or cached answer, then region fallback. We ship cost simulations for your traffic shape so you can agree on thresholds during the pilot."
   - Practical win: "We already reduced a pilot customer's batch cost by ~30% on their busiest flows with minimal quality impact."

Suggested 6‑slide rapid deck (for micro-demos / pilot kickoff) — slide titles and 1–2 bullets per slide:
- Slide 1: "Why inference reliability matters to your product" — 1–2 customer pain bullets + two metrics to baseline (p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens).
- Slide 2: "How Redwood approaches serving" — diagram text: runtime + routing + caching + model catalog (keep simple).
- Slide 3: "Pilot plan (48–72h)" — what we measure, quick integrations: SDK + sample traffic, knob list.
- Slide 4: "Canary + fallback ladder" — the four-step fallback ladder and who owns each step.
- Slide 5: "Expected outcomes & success criteria" — e.g., p95 latency <= target OR cost reduction >= 20% w/ quality delta < 2% on curated evals.
- Slide 6: "Next steps & ask" — trial token access, data sharing checklist, timeline.

Battlecard snippets (quick pasteable lines)
- Competitor angle: "LLM cloud A sells managed endpoints but no unified private runtime — their fallback options are manual and often require juggling infra teams."
- Quick SE reply: "We provide the same API and routing controls across all deployment modes, so fallbacks are policy-driven not manual ops."
- Cost objection: "Their unit price looks cheaper." — SE reply: "We model your traffic and show end-to-end cost including caching & batching; for many workloads the effective per-interaction cost is lower once you account for batching gains and reduced repeat prompts."
- Security request: "We need VPC + KMS + audit logs." — SE reply: "Private deployments include a customer-managed control plane option and integrations with major KMS/HSM providers; we can scope an on-prem package for the pilot if needed."

Canary checklist (mini runbook, 7 items)
- Define canary slice (e.g., 5% of production traffic or 2 internal CI endpoints)
- Baseline metrics captured (p95 latency, token cost, failure rate, rouge/accuracy on eval set)
- Rollout policy configured (time window, automatic rollback delta, fallback model mapping)
- Observe period (48h min for traffic variability)
- Smoke tests (synthetic prompts covering worst-case sequences)
- Stakeholders for rollback decision (SE, infra lead, product manager)
- Post-mortem template link (Confluence)

Quick objection bank (phrases + one-line counters)
- "We already run our models on cloud GPUs." -> "Great — Redwood plugs into that flow and focuses on production economics: fewer head-hours wasted, more efficient batch scheduling, and predictable tail latency so your product features don't degrade at peak."
- "We're worried about latency with quantized models." -> "We benchmark and propose quantization only where quality impact is minimal; fallback policies let you switch to the full model for critical queries."
- "This sounds like extra ops overhead." -> "Our Console surfaces the common ops (routing, rollouts, cost sim) in UI + APIs. For most pilots we do the heavy lifting and hand off after the first month."

Speaker notes / quick cues for SEs (to memorize)
- Opening: "We're focused on two things: predictable user experience and predictable costs. If we can hit a measurable improvement on one we call it a success."
- If they ask for numbers: have one anonymized example from an enterprise pilot and a 'typical' pilot outcome for mid-market.
- When they push tech: redirect to a technical deep-dive session with infra engineering + solutions.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self)
- Collect two anonymized pilot numbers from last 6 months to replace generic claims. (Priya)
- Capture a short GIF of canary rollback flow to embed in slide 4. (Marco)
- Validate the cost-sim numbers for small-batch versus continuous-batch workloads and add a one-slide simulation template. (Noah)
- Decide final naming: "fallback ladder" vs "degradation ladder" across all GTM artifacts.

Tone & usage guidance
- This doc is for rapid SE prep before a pilot kickoff or a 20–30m intro call. Keep 1–2 lines of evidence for each point and never more than three metrics on a slide. Use customer stories sparingly and only when you can cite numbers.

Appendix (clipboard assets for copy/paste)
- Short pitch line: "Redwood Inference: predictable LLM serving with built‑in fallbacks and cost simulations — same API everywhere."
- Meeting CTA: "If we can baseline your p95 and token profile in 48h, we can run a pilot that shows either latency improvement or cost savings within 2 weeks."
- Link stash: Confluence pilot template / JIRA pilot epic / sample SDK snippet.

End of draft — save as 'threepoint-engineer-seller-cheat-briefing-v0.1' when we land the anonymized numbers.

NOTES TO SELF: keep this doc <1 page when printed. Keep bullets short.
